abstract: Abstract Hypoxia enhances histone methylation by inhibiting oxygen- and α-ketoglutarate-dependent demethylases, resulting in increased methylated histones. This study reveals how hypoxia-induced methylation affects histone clipping and the reorganization of heterochromatin into senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHF) during oncogene-induced senescence (OIS) in IMR90 human fibroblasts. Notably, using top-down proteomics, we discovered specific cleavage sites targeted by Cathepsin L (CTSL) in H3, H2B and H4 during Raf activation, identifying novel sites in H2B and H4. Hypoxia counteracts CTSL-mediated histone clipping by promoting methylation without affecting CTSL’s activity. This increase in methylation under hypoxia protects against clipping, reshaping the epigenetic landscape and influencing chromatin accessibility, as shown by ATAC-seq analysis. These insights underscore the pivotal role of hypoxia-induced histone methylation in protecting chromatin from significant epigenetic shifts during cellular aging.

Materials and methods
Cell culture
Human lung fibroblast IMR90 cells (CCL-186, ATCC, Manassas, VA, USA) were cultured in Eagle's minimum essential medium (10–009, Corning, Glendale, AZ, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 IU/ml penicillin, and 100 μg/ml streptomycin. Cells were cultured in humidified air containing 5% CO
2
at 37 °C. Cells were incubated under hypoxic conditions in a Forma anaerobic incubator (Model 1029, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) in an atmosphere of 5% CO
2
, 95% N
2
, and 0.5% O
2
.
Generating stable cell lines using retroviral or lentiviral infection
IMR90 cells were infected with a retrovirus encoding ΔB-RAF:ER obtained from Dr. Martin McMahon (University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA) to generate IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER cells. The ΔB-RAF:ER fusion protein comprises a B-RAF (449–804 aa) protein kinase domain and a mutant form of the hormone-binding domain of the estrogen receptor (ER) (281–599 aa, with a single amino acid change from glycine to arginine at position 525) engineered to be nonresponsive to β-estradiol but responsive to 4-hydroxy-tamoxifen (4-OHT) (
3
,
27
). Infecting IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER cells with lentiviruses expressing Myc-His-tagged M56 CTSL or an empty vector, using the pLenti CMV vector system, generated IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER-M56CTSL and IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER EV cells, respectively. IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER-shCTSL and IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER-shScramble cells were generated by infecting IMR90-ΔB-RAF:ER cells with lentiviruses encoding shRNA against human CTSL (5′-GGTGGTTGGCTACGGATTTGA-3′) and scramble (control) (5′- CCTAAGGTTAAGTCGCCCTCG-3′), respectively, using the pLKO.1 lentiviral vector system (Addgene, Cambridge, MA, USA). A list of the stable cell lines generated is summarized in
Supplementary Table S1
.
Reagents and antibodies
A list of the antibodies and reagents used is provided in
Supplementary Tables S2
and
S3
.
Senescence-associated β-galactosidase assay
Senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) activity was measured as previously described (
28
). The percentage of SA-β-gal-positive cells (blue staining) was calculated as the number of SA-β-gal-positive cells divided by the total number of cells. Counts were performed in at least three randomly selected microscopic fields from two independent experiments to determine the mean percentage of positively stained cells.
Quantitative reverse transcription-PCR
Steady-state mRNA expression was measured using quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), as described previously (
3
). The pairs of forward and reverse primer sequences for qRT-PCR were as follows: human cathepsin L (F) 5′-AAACTGGGAGGCTTATCTCACT-3′ / I 5′-GCATAATCCA TTAGGCCACC–T-3′ and 18S rRNA (F) 5′-ACCGCAGCTAGGAATAATGGAATA-3′ / 5′-CTTTCGCTCTGGTCCGTC–T-3′.
Immunofluorescence microscopy and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci quantification
The cells were labeled with the indicated primary and secondary antibodies conjugated to Alexa Fluor
®
488 or 546 (Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA) as previously described (
29
). The cells were mounted on coverslips with Hoechst 33 258 and observed under a Zeiss LSM800 inverted confocal microscope (Carl Zeiss, Thornwood, NY, USA), according to the manufacturer's instructions. The primary antibodies used for immunofluorescence are summarized in
Supplementary Table S2
. The degree of senescence-associated heterochromatin foci (SAHFs) was quantified using the Hoechst coefficient of variation (CV) or H3K9me3 intensity (
30
). The CV was calculated as the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean intensity of Hoechst or H3K9me3 using ImageJ software that identifies Hoechst- and H3K9me3-stained nuclei. The CV is presented as boxplots. The midline of the boxplot represents the median, the bottom of the box represents the 25th percentile, the top of the box represents the 75th percentile, and the whiskers represent the minimum and maximum values.
Chromatin fraction and histone acid extraction
Cellular total histones were prepared from cells as described previously (
31
). The cells were lysed by using hypotonic lysis buffer [150 mM NaCl, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS, 50mM Tris-HCl (pH7.4), 50 mM beta-glycerophosphate, 25 mM sodium fluoride, 20 mM ethylene glycol tetra-acetic acid, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 1 mM sodium orthovanandate, 1% igepal, 0.5 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride, 1 μg/ml aprotinin and leupeptin] for 10 min on ice. The cell lysates were collected by centrifugation at 500 g for 10 min. The nuclear pellets were washed and lysed with a hypotonic lysis buffer for 40 min on ice. The chromatin fraction was recovered by centrifugation at 1500 g for 5 min. For histone acid extraction, the chromatin fraction was resuspended with 0.4 N H
2
SO
4
for 90 min in ice. The samples were centrifuged at 16 000 g for 15 min, and the supernatant was incubated with 1 ml acetone for overnight at −20°C. The histone was collected by centrifugation at 16 000 g for 15 min. After washing with acetone, the histone pellet was dried and then resuspended with an appropriate buffer for the subsequent following reaction. For detecting histone modifications, we employed histone acid extraction techniques for both top-down proteomics and western blot analyses.
Top-down proteomic analyses
The histone pellets isolated as described above were air-dried for 10 min and resuspended in 100 μl of ddH
2
O instead of 4 M urea. The histone protein concentration was measured using the BCA assay (23 225, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins were aliquoted into several tubes for top-down and western blot analyses and freeze-dried. Top-down analysis was performed using a Q Exactive HF-X mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a dual online liquid chromatography (LC) system based on a nanoACQUITY (Waters, Milford, MA, USA) with a dual online LC system, at the Center for Proteogenome Research, as previously described (
32
). Briefly, two analytical columns (75 μm × 100 cm, packed) and two solid-phase extraction columns (150 μm × 3 cm) packed with MAbPac particles (C8 resin, 4 μm diameter, 300-Å pore size; Thermo Fisher Scientific) were used. Each histone sample (400 ng) from four different conditions was separated using a 120-min gradient (25–35% solvent B over 101 min, 35–80% over 5 min, 80% for 10 min and holding at 1% for 4 min). Solvents A and B comprised 0.1% formic acid in water and 0.1% formic acid IACN, respectively. The column flow rate was 600 nl/min. The Q Exactive HF-X was tuned by setting the trapping gas pre-setting value to 0.2 to maintain the ultra-high vacuum range under 5.0 × 10
−11
. The eluted proteins were ionized at an electric potential of 2.7 kV, and the desolvation capillary temperature was 300°C. Full mass spectrometry (MS) scans were acquired with an m/z range of 500 to 2 000 and a resolution of 120 000. The maximum ion injection time and target values for automatic gain control (AGC) were 250 ms and 5.0 × 10
6
, respectively. For multiplexed MS/MS scans, ions of the same protein but with different charges (up to six) were simultaneously isolated and fragmented at a resolution of 60 000. Multiplexed MS/MS of an intact protein showed increased sequence-specific fragments, thereby increasing sequence coverage. The AGC target value and maximum ion injection time for multiplexed ions were 5.0 × 10
6
and 125 ms, respectively. One full MS scan and 20 targeted MS/MS scans were repeated during a 120 min run time. The number of micro-scan and normalized collision energy were 3 and 25, respectively, and the isolation window was 0.6 Th. The LC-MS/MS data were analyzed using FLASHDeconv2D to obtain monoisotopic masses from the MS spectra, and MODplus was used for annotating multiplexed MS/MS spectra (
33
,
34
). VisioProt-MS was used to construct a 2D feature map based on the monoisotopic masses obtained from FLASHDecov2D (
35
).
In vitro CTSL reaction
In vitro
proteolytic reaction of rCTSL (50 pg) was performed with recombinant histones (200 ng) at 37 °C for 30 min in 20 μl of reaction buffer comprising 50 mM MES pH 5.5 containing 5 mM DTT, 1 mM EDTA, and 0.005% Brij-35. We isolated the histone acid extracts from IMR90 cells cultured under hypoxia or normoxia to obtain endogenous histones, as previously described (
36
). For each
in vitro
proteolytic reaction, the histone acid extract (500 ng) was treated with 0.01 to 0.2 ng of rCTSL in 20 μl of reaction buffer (MES buffer pH 5.5) for 30 min at 37°C.
Cellular CTSL activity analysis
We used the Magic Red Cathepsin L Detection Kit (Immunochemistry Technologies, Bloomington, MN, USA) to measure the intracellular CTSL activity in whole living cells. Briefly, 5000 suspended cells were loaded with Magic Red Cathepsin L reagent containing a CTSL substrate, N-carbobenzyloxy-Phe-Arg-MR-Arg-Phe (MR-FR
2
), for each enzymatic reaction. The fluorescence was then measured (Ex 590 nm, Em 630 nm) using the kinetic mode of SpectraMax® iD3 (Molecular Devices) at 37 °C for 30–90 min using the bottom-read function. The enzyme reaction velocity (Reactive fluorescence unit (RFU)/min) was determined using GraphPad Prism software (GraphPad Software, version 8.0) using a linear regression function.
Competitive enzyme kinetic assay
Recombinant human cathepsin L (rCTSL) (catalog #952-CY) and fluorogenic peptide substrate VII: Z-Leu-Arg-4-methyl-7-coumarylamide (Z-LR-AMC) (catalog #ES008) were purchased from R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN, USA). The enzymatic reactions were initiated upon adding rCTSL (96 pM) to nine different Z-LR-AMC concentrations (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 μM) in 100 μl of assay buffer (50 mM MES (pH 5.5), 5 mM DTT, 1 mM EDTA, and 0.005% Brij-35). The detail methods are described in the Supplementary Information.
Molecular dynamics simulations
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed with OpenMM software and CHARMM36m force field (
37–47
). The crystal structure of the CTSL C25A mutant with Gln-Leu-Ala peptides (Protein Data Bank ID 3K24) was used to model the CTSL systems. The mutated Ala25 residue was modified back to Cys25, and only one monomer of the original dimer structure was used in the simulation because the active site was far from the interfacial region between the monomers. The protonation states of 71, 109, 9, 50, 119, 140 and 163 residues in the enzyme were calculated with Propka3.1 at pH 5.5. In the MD simulations, two different 6-residue H3 fragments (H3
19-24
) were used as the substrates: naïve H3
19-24
and tri-methylated H3
19-24
K23me3 (
39
,
40
). The detail methods are described in the Supplementary Information.
Transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing assay
The transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) library was constructed from 50 000 nuclei from each cell group using a Tn5-Nextera DNA library prep kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) (
48
). Transposed DNA was purified using the MinElute PCR Purification kit (QIAGEN, Germantown, MD, USA). DNA fragments were amplified through PCR using Nextera index primers 1 and 2 (Illumina) and tagmented DNA. Libraries were assessed for fragment length distribution on a Bioanalyzer High-Sensitivity DNA Chip (Agilent Genomics, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Indexed libraries were then sequenced by Macrogen (Seoul, Republic of Korea) using the HiSeq X-10 sequencer (Illumina).
ATAC-seq data analysis
ATAC-seq data analyses were performed as previously described (
https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/epigenetics/tutorials/atac-seq/tutorial.html
) (
49
). The presence of the Nextera adapters was checked using FastQC (
http://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/

50
). Low-quality bases (base quality score < 20) at the ends of the reads and short reads (< 20 bp) were removed. The trimmed paired-end reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg38) for read mapping using Bowtie2 with default parameters (
51
). The maximum fragment length was extended to 1000 bp to observe valid read pairs and to allow dovetailing of read pairs. After mapping, the output BAM file was filtered using Samtools (
52
). After mitochondrial DNA was removed, the properly paired reads of nuclear DNA were obtained with high mapping quality (MAPQ score ≥ 30). Duplicate reads were removed, and the size distribution of the properly paired reads was obtained using Picard (
https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/
). BigWig files were created using Deeptools bamCoverage with the option –normalizeUsing RPKM to visualize the read coverages using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (
53
,
54
). For peak calling, the BAM file was converted to the BED format using Bedtools (
55
) to re-center the signal of each read on the 5′ read start site where Tn5 cuts. The peaks were then called using MACS2 with parameters –format BED –nomodel –shift -100 –extsize 200 (
56
). Overlapping or adjoined peaks were merged, and the peak regions for each condition were classified. Differential peaks (adjusted
P
-value < 0.05, abs (log
2
FC) > 1) were identified using DESeq2 (
57
). The correlations and principal component analysis (PCA) plots of all experimental samples were then plotted using Deeptools and ggplot2 package in R. Reads per kilobase per million mapped reads (RPKM) in differential peaks were computed, and a heatmap was plotted using Morpheus (
https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus
) to view significant peaks in each condition. The differential peaks were annotated to each genomic component using ChIPseeker with the TSS-defined option (-1 kb to + 100 bp) (
58
).
ChIP-seq data analysis
Ras
-activated and -inactivated IMR90 cell lamin B1 ChIP-seq data were imported from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (
GSE49341
) (
59
). ChIP-seq reads were aligned to the hg38 reference genome using Bowtie2 with default parameters. The BAM file was filtered using Samtools to obtain reads with high mapping quality (MAPQ score ≥ 20) and Picard was used to remove duplicated reads. Lamin B1-associated domains (LADs) were detected using RSEG mode 2 versus input data (
60
).
Combining ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data analysis
The hg38 genome assembly was divided into 10 kb bins, and the X and Y chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA were removed. ATAC-seq reads with a small fragment size (<100 bp) were used to indicate nucleosome-free regions (NFRs), and the RPKM in each bin was computed. We first computed the portion of each bin overlapping with the LAD peaks and defined LAD bins as the bins with >50% of this score to identify them. The two data sets were combined based on the 10 kb bins, and the bins with an NFR RPKM value of 0 for all samples were excluded.
Transposase-accessible chromatin with visualization assay
Cells were fixed and treated with the fluorescent Atto-590 attached Tn5 (Atto-590 Tn5) for 30 min at 37°C. The cells were washed, co-stained with H3K9me3 or H3K4me3 antibodies, and mounted with Hoechst 33 258 (
61
). The fluorescence intensity of the Atto-590 fluorescence signal in the nucleus was measured using ImageJ software and is presented as boxplots. Pearson's correlation coefficient of transposase-accessible chromatin with visualization (ATAC-see) signals (Atto590 intensity) with H3K9me3 signals (Alexa 488 intensity) was obtained using Volocity software (PerkinElmer) as previously described.

Introduction
Hypoxia, a state of low oxygen availability, plays a pivotal role in regulating cell senescence (
1
) and differentiation (
2–4
) by modulating the activity of specific genes critical for various cellular functions, including glycolysis, angiogenesis, cell adhesion, metastasis and proliferation. Central to this regulatory mechanism is the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) α/β, a transcription factor that activates around half of these hypoxia-responsive genes (
5
). Under normal oxygen conditions (normoxia), HIF-1α undergoes hydroxylation, leading to its inactivation. This process is mediated by specific prolyl and asparaginyl hydroxylases that require oxygen and α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) to function (
4
,
5
). However, in hypoxia, these hydroxylation reactions are halted, resulting in the activation of HIF-1α. Furthermore, hypoxia influences epigenetic modifications, particularly histone methylation. Several oxygen- and α-KG-dependent demethylases, Jumonji domain-containing histone lysine demethylases (JHDMs/KDMs), which are responsible for removing methyl groups from histones, are inhibited under hypoxia, leading to an increase in methylated histones (
6
,
7
). This increase inhistone methylation status has immediate and direct effects on chromatin structure and function, illustrating the profound impact of hypoxia on cellular fate through both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms.
The ENCODE project has significantly contributed to our comprehension of this complex epigenetic landscape by systematically cataloging histone modifications, along with chromatin accessibility and gene expression profiles, across numerous tissues and cell types (
8
). Such detailed mapping has highlighted the critical roles of specific modifications, like Histone 3 lysine 4 tri-methylation (H3K4me3), H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, in demarcating euchromatic and heterochromatic regions. For example, H3K4me3 and H3Kac, indicators of active transcription, are predominantly located at transcription start sites of genes within accessible euchromatin. In contrast, H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 mark the promoters of silenced genes, characteristic of the densely packed heterochromatin (
9
,
10
).
Recent studies have revealed that the N-terminus of histone H3 undergoes cleavage in various species and cellular contexts, including mouse intestinal villi, human monocytes, yeast sporulation, and the neuronal differentiation of stem cells (
11–13
). This phenomenon, known as histone clipping, represents a significant, albeit rare, post-translational modification. Unless counteracted by the synthesis of new histones, histone clipping is irreversible, marking it as a critical event in certain key cellular processes (
14–16
). Notably, this modification frequently occurs during irreversible cellular events, such as terminal differentiation and oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), highlighting its potential role in steering cell fate and development.
OIS, triggered by the enforced activation of oncogenes like Ras, Raf, and Myc in primary cells, leads to rapid cellular aging by engaging the p53 and Rb tumor suppressor pathways (
17
). This process has been observed in human melanocytic nevi, where cells harboring a high proportion of the B-RAF V600E mutation enter senescence, thereby acting as a surveillance system to thwart tumor progression. Such Raf-induced senescence effectively prevents the expansion of oncogenic cells in early tumor development (
18
,
19
). Nonetheless, OIS paradoxically promotes the secretion of inflammatory factors, creating an environment that may predispose to cancer development. Thus, OIS exhibits both tumor-suppressing and tumor-promoting effects, a duality that underscores the complexity of cellular responses to oncogene activation (
18
).
The concept of deepening senescence has been supported by various observations, including cell cycle arrest, a persistent DNA damage response, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, chromatin decompaction, histone loss and reduced Lamin B levels (
19
,
20
). However, the cause-and-effect relationships and the chronological sequence of these senescent phenotypes remain unclear. OIS prompts a significant increase in active cathepsin L (CTSL), a lysosomal cysteine protease, within the nucleus (
21
,
22
). This elevation leads to the proteolytic clipping of histone H3, signaling profound epigenetic alterations that include changes in chromatin structure. In parallel, hypoxia attenuates senescence through influencing key processes such as the DNA damage response, cell cycle regulation and the AMPK-mTOR signaling pathway (
23–26
). This study pioneers in exploring how hypoxia-induced enhancements in histone methylation might influence epigenetic phenomena, including histone clipping and the redistribution of heterochromatin during OIS, potentially counteracting senescence.
Our study unveils a novel finding, using top-down proteomics to identify the specific cleavage sites in H2B and H4, in addition to H3, during senescence induced by Raf activation. This marks the first report of CTSL’s broad specificity across multiple histone types. Remarkably, hypoxic conditions prevent the clipping of all three histones not by directly inhibiting CTSL activity, per se, but through the upregulation of specific histone methylation marks near the sites of cleavage that results in decreased histone cleavage. This indicates a specific role of hypoxia in protecting histones from proteolytic cleavage by maintaining methylation states, thereby impacting cell fate decisions.

Recombinant human cathepsin L (rCTSL) (catalog #952-CY) and fluorogenic peptide substrate VII: Z-Leu-Arg-4-methyl-7-coumarylamide (Z-LR-AMC) (catalog #ES008) were purchased from R&D Systems (Minneapolis, MN, USA). The enzymatic reactions were initiated upon adding rCTSL (96 pM) to nine different Z-LR-AMC concentrations (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 μM) in 100 μl of assay buffer (50 mM MES (pH 5.5), 5 mM DTT, 1 mM EDTA, and 0.005% Brij-35). The detail methods are described in the Supplementary Information.

Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were performed with OpenMM software and CHARMM36m force field (
37–47
). The crystal structure of the CTSL C25A mutant with Gln-Leu-Ala peptides (Protein Data Bank ID 3K24) was used to model the CTSL systems. The mutated Ala25 residue was modified back to Cys25, and only one monomer of the original dimer structure was used in the simulation because the active site was far from the interfacial region between the monomers. The protonation states of 71, 109, 9, 50, 119, 140 and 163 residues in the enzyme were calculated with Propka3.1 at pH 5.5. In the MD simulations, two different 6-residue H3 fragments (H3
19-24
) were used as the substrates: naïve H3
19-24
and tri-methylated H3
19-24
K23me3 (
39
,
40
). The detail methods are described in the Supplementary Information.
Transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing assay
The transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) library was constructed from 50 000 nuclei from each cell group using a Tn5-Nextera DNA library prep kit (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA) (
48
). Transposed DNA was purified using the MinElute PCR Purification kit (QIAGEN, Germantown, MD, USA). DNA fragments were amplified through PCR using Nextera index primers 1 and 2 (Illumina) and tagmented DNA. Libraries were assessed for fragment length distribution on a Bioanalyzer High-Sensitivity DNA Chip (Agilent Genomics, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Indexed libraries were then sequenced by Macrogen (Seoul, Republic of Korea) using the HiSeq X-10 sequencer (Illumina).
ATAC-seq data analysis
ATAC-seq data analyses were performed as previously described (
https://training.galaxyproject.org/training-material/topics/epigenetics/tutorials/atac-seq/tutorial.html
) (
49
). The presence of the Nextera adapters was checked using FastQC (
http://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/
), and the adapter sequence of paired-end reads (CTGTCTCTTATACACATCTCCGAGCCCACGAGAC, CTGTCTCTTATACACATCTGACGCTGCCGACGA) was removed using Cutadapt (
50
). Low-quality bases (base quality score < 20) at the ends of the reads and short reads (< 20 bp) were removed. The trimmed paired-end reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg38) for read mapping using Bowtie2 with default parameters (
51
). The maximum fragment length was extended to 1000 bp to observe valid read pairs and to allow dovetailing of read pairs. After mapping, the output BAM file was filtered using Samtools (
52
). After mitochondrial DNA was removed, the properly paired reads of nuclear DNA were obtained with high mapping quality (MAPQ score ≥ 30). Duplicate reads were removed, and the size distribution of the properly paired reads was obtained using Picard (
https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/
). BigWig files were created using Deeptools bamCoverage with the option –normalizeUsing RPKM to visualize the read coverages using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (
53
,
54
). For peak calling, the BAM file was converted to the BED format using Bedtools (
55
) to re-center the signal of each read on the 5′ read start site where Tn5 cuts. The peaks were then called using MACS2 with parameters –format BED –nomodel –shift -100 –extsize 200 (
56
). Overlapping or adjoined peaks were merged, and the peak regions for each condition were classified. Differential peaks (adjusted
P
-value < 0.05, abs (log
2
FC) > 1) were identified using DESeq2 (
57
). The correlations and principal component analysis (PCA) plots of all experimental samples were then plotted using Deeptools and ggplot2 package in R. Reads per kilobase per million mapped reads (RPKM) in differential peaks were computed, and a heatmap was plotted using Morpheus (
https://software.broadinstitute.org/morpheus
) to view significant peaks in each condition. The differential peaks were annotated to each genomic component using ChIPseeker with the TSS-defined option (-1 kb to + 100 bp) (
58
).
ChIP-seq data analysis
Ras
-activated and -inactivated IMR90 cell lamin B1 ChIP-seq data were imported from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (
GSE49341
) (
59
). ChIP-seq reads were aligned to the hg38 reference genome using Bowtie2 with default parameters. The BAM file was filtered using Samtools to obtain reads with high mapping quality (MAPQ score ≥ 20) and Picard was used to remove duplicated reads. Lamin B1-associated domains (LADs) were detected using RSEG mode 2 versus input data (
60
).
Combining ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq data analysis
The hg38 genome assembly was divided into 10 kb bins, and the X and Y chromosomes and mitochondrial DNA were removed. ATAC-seq reads with a small fragment size (<100 bp) were used to indicate nucleosome-free regions (NFRs), and the RPKM in each bin was computed. We first computed the portion of each bin overlapping with the LAD peaks and defined LAD bins as the bins with >50% of this score to identify them. The two data sets were combined based on the 10 kb bins, and the bins with an NFR RPKM value of 0 for all samples were excluded.
Transposase-accessible chromatin with visualization assay
Cells were fixed and treated with the fluorescent Atto-590 attached Tn5 (Atto-590 Tn5) for 30 min at 37°C. The cells were washed, co-stained with H3K9me3 or H3K4me3 antibodies, and mounted with Hoechst 33 258 (
61
). The fluorescence intensity of the Atto-590 fluorescence signal in the nucleus was measured using ImageJ software and is presented as boxplots. Pearson's correlation coefficient of transposase-accessible chromatin with visualization (ATAC-see) signals (Atto590 intensity) with H3K9me3 signals (Alexa 488 intensity) was obtained using Volocity software (PerkinElmer) as previously described.

Discussion
Within stem cell niches and solid tumors, hypoxia stalls cellular senescence and differentiation, preserving the quiescent and undifferentiated state of stem cells (
70
). The deletion of HIF-1α is associated with accelerated cellular senescence (
1–4
). Beyond its role in activating HIF pathways, hypoxia indirectly promotes the accumulation of methylated histones by suppressing the enzymatic functions of oxygen- and α-ketoglutarate-dependent histone demethylases (JHDMs/KDMs) (
1–4
). Our research focused on the repercussions of elevated levels of methylated histones observed in hypoxia for other epigenetic changes, notably histone clipping and heterochromatin redistribution during OIS. This study reveals a novel mechanism through which hypoxia influences cell fate decisions by increasing methylated histones, which protect histones and chromatin from significant epigenetic alterations.
Our findings reveal that, similar to hypoxia, KDM pan-inhibitors like JIB-04, which elevate methylated histone levels, effectively protect against histone clipping during OIS. Conversely, methyltransferase inhibitors such as AdOX reduce methylated histone levels, even in hypoxic conditions, leading to increased histone clipping under hypoxia (
63
). Unlike hypoxia, however, neither KDM nor CTSL inhibition prevents OIS from inducing SAHF formation and SA-β-gal activation (data not shown). In contrast, histone methyltransferase inhibitors are sufficient to induce SAHF formation and SA-β-gal activation, even in hypoxic conditions (Figure
6
). These findings suggest that while elevated levels of methylated histones are necessary, they are not sufficient on their own to replicate the effects of hypoxia in bypassing OIS.
An
in vitro
enzyme kinetic assay (Figure
5
) revealed that methylation at H3K23 and H3K18 increased the Ki values against CTSL. However, it remains unclear whether this increase in Ki is sufficient to protect H3 from CTSL cleavage or if methylation at these sites recruits proteins that shield the CTSL cleavage sites. Notably, histone peptide microarray analyses revealed that dimethylation or trimethylation at H3K23 (H3K23me2/3) promotes specific interactions with proteins containing chromodomains and double Tudor domains (
71
,
72
). These interactions suggest a protective mechanism in which H3K23me2/3 recruits these protein domains, effectively shielding the histone H3 cleavage sites—particularly between H3A21 and H3T22—from cathepsin L (CTSL) activity. Middle-down proteomic (
73
) and ChIP-seq analyses (
74
) have shown a positive correlation between H3K23 methylation and established heterochromatin markers, including H3K9me3 and H3K27me3, as well as heterochromatin-associated proteins. This correlation suggests that H3K23 methylation plays a crucial role in organizing the genome within heterochromatin structures, rendering histone tails less accessible and thus indirectly protecting them from cleavage by CTSL. (
75
). While our findings highlight a protective role for methylation in shielding histones from CTSL activity, it is needed to consider that alternative regulatory pathways may influence histone clipping, including overall CTSL levels. Although hypoxia did not alter the total CTSL activity in OIS cells, as measured using a synthetic substrate, it reduces the levels of mature nuclear CTSL (Figure
3C
and
4C
). Further investigation is warranted to determine whether other nuclear CTSL targets, such as a transcription factor CDP/Cux (
76
,
77
) and p53BP1 (
78
), respond differently to reduced nuclear CTSL levels under hypoxic conditions. The observation that ectopic expression of cleaved H3.3 (H3.3cs1) is sufficient to induce senescence in IMR90 cells suggests that histone clipping contributes to senescence processes, creating a positive feedback loop that further reinforces senescence (
22
) (72. 73). Hypoxic conditions disrupt this feedback cycle by preventing histone clipping through the increased histone methylation, thereby limiting the progression of senescence.
Sati
et al.
employed a polymer model of a chromosome to quantitatively evaluate the mechanical forces that drive SAHF formation during OIS (
79
). They identified that for SAHF to form, the interaction strength between the nuclear lamina and heterochromatin must diminish. Consequently, histone clipping, which removes heterochromatin markers like H3K9me3 from the N-terminus, likely weakens this crucial interaction. In OIS, degradation occurs not only in histones but also in the nuclear lamina (
59
,
69
). Our unpublished data reveal that hypoxia prevents the degradation of both histones and the nuclear lamina during OIS, suggesting a protective mechanism. Unlike hypoxia, KDM inhibitors such as JIB-04 fail to prevent SAHF formation since they do not safeguard the nuclear lamina during OIS. Moreover, while OIS leads to a wrinkled nuclear lamina and a degraded cytoskeleton, hypoxic conditions preserve the integrity of both the nuclear lamina and the cytoskeleton. The role of hypoxia in maintaining the strength of the interaction between the nuclear lamina and heterochromatin warrants further investigation.
Our ATAC-seq analysis demonstrated that Raf activation enhances chromatin accessibility, an effect significantly mitigated under hypoxic conditions. However, the precise relationship between SAHF formation and chromatin accessibility remains to be fully understood. By correlating ATAC-seq data with lamin B1 ChIP-seq analysis (
59
), we noted an increase in NFRs only in LAD-free regions (group 3 in Figures
8F
and
9A
) during OIS, not within LAD regions (
61
). Investigating how hypoxia preserves LADs to inhibit SAHF formation during OIS is crucial for a deeper understanding of these mechanisms.
During OIS, we noted a decrease in methylation at H3K4, H3K9, H3K27, and H3K36, attributable to the activation of specific histone demethylases: KDM5/JARID1 (H3K4me1/2/3 demethylases) (
80
), KDM4/JMJD2 (H3K9me1/2/3 and H3K36me1/2/3 demethylases) (
81
), and KDM6/JMJD3 (H3K27me1/2/3 demethylases) (
82
,
83
). Concurrently, expression of certain methyltransferases, including EZH2, a key component of the H3K27-specific methyltransferase complex, diminishes during OIS (
84
). This trend highlights a broader pattern of demethylation affecting various histone residues throughout OIS. Notably, levels of H3K23me3 and H3K18me3 also decline during OIS, yet the enzymes directly responsible for modifying these particular residues remain unidentified. The presence of methylated H3K23 and H3K18 residues, initially found in the heterochromatin of Tetrahymena thermophila (
64
,
85
) and later in Caenorhabditis elegans (
73
), has been detailed in human cancer cells through recent MS advances (
86
). Furthermore, point mutations at these residues have been noted in various cancers, underscoring the need to clarify their contribution to oncogenesis (
65
).
In human monocytes, three proteases, neutrophil serine proteases, cathepsin G, and neutrophil elastase, specifically cleave the H3 N-terminus between alanine 21 and threonine 22 (
12
). ChIP-seq analysis with an H3cs1-specific antibody demonstrated H3cs1’s enrichment in open chromatin and transcription start sites (TSS) of active genes (
13
). Deleting these three proteases in human monocytes halted H3 cleavage and enhanced chromatin accessibility at TSSs. This suggests that these proteolytic enzymes target histones within open, accessible chromatin rather than within dense heterochromatin regions. Supporting this, our ATAC-seq analysis shows a preference for histone clipping in more accessible euchromatin regions, indicating a selective cleavage by proteases in these areas over condensed heterochromatin regions like LADs. These insights reveal a previously unexplored pathway through which hypoxia influences cell fate, by promoting histone methylation that guards against extensive epigenetic alterations.
